title: Autism, complex needs, EHC plans and reasonable adjustments
blurb: Make reasonable adjustments for autistic and disabled children, communicate in their preferred way, and explain how EHC plans work under the SEND Code and NICE NG213.
question: Ethan, 7, is autistic and is admitted for surgery tomorrow. His father says Ethan becomes very distressed by noise, bright lights and unexpected changes. Which plan best reflects reasonable adjustments?

teach.body: Neurodiversity means brains work in different ways; autism and ADHD are examples. Some children also have severe complex needs from disability or long-term illness. Formally, the Equality Act 2010 s20 requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people, and NICE NG213 sets out joined-up education, health and social care for disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs. Plain English: change how you work so the child can get the same quality of care, and ask the child and family what works.
teach.cite: Equality Act 2010 s20; NICE NG213 (2022, updated 2023)

cells.label: Visual timetable, first on the list

teach.caption: Parents are experts in their child: use their knowledge of routines, triggers and comforts.

teach.body: Find out which communication formats the child prefers, for example augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) such as symbols for a child who does not use speech, and use that format. A child may prefer different formats for different purposes. Ask if they have an up-to-date communication passport, and record preferences in a shareable way so they do not have to repeat themselves.

teach.h: Signs that need a closer look

rows.label: Regression in language or social skills
Change in behaviour in a non-verbal child

teach.note: NICE CG128 1.3.1: refer children under 3 with regression in language or social skills to the autism team. NG213 1.4.17: reassess if needs change significantly.

teach.text: Do not assume new distress or self-injury in an autistic child is 'just the autism'. This is diagnostic overshadowing: a child who cannot say they are in pain may show it through behaviour. Look for a physical cause first, such as pain, constipation, infection or a dental problem.

teach.h: Scenario: Ava, 9, before a blood test
teach.body: Ava is autistic and does not use speech; she uses a picture symbol book. Nurse Femi asks her mother which symbols Ava knows, then uses the book to show each step: sit on Mum's lap, cold cream, small scratch, plaster, sticker. She books a quiet room and the first appointment to avoid waiting, gives Ava time to look at each picture, and records what helped in her communication passport.

items: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty (Equality Act s20), not a favour.
Use the child's preferred communication format; ask about a communication passport.
EHC plan: legal local authority plan, birth to 25, final plan within 20 weeks of the request.
Professionals give advice within 6 weeks; plans are reviewed at least every 12 months.
Record the child's views in their own words; look for physical causes of new distress.

summary: You can now plan reasonable adjustments for an autistic or disabled child and communicate in their preferred format. You can also explain what an EHC plan is, its timescales, and how to contribute to it in line with NG213 and the SEND Code.

A.q: Ethan, 7, is autistic and is admitted for surgery tomorrow. His father says Ethan becomes very distressed by noise, bright lights and unexpected changes. Which plan best reflects reasonable adjustments?
options: A bay near the nurses' station for close watching
A quiet side room, visual timetable and his routines
Sedation on admission to keep him calm
The usual ward routine so he gets used to it
A.why: Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act s20) include a quiet environment, visual preparation, predictable routines and using the family's knowledge.

whyNot.0: A busy area near the station adds noise and light.
whyNot.2: Sedation is not a first-line adjustment for sensory needs.
whyNot.3: Keeping the usual routine fails the duty to adjust.

A.q: A parent asks what an education, health and care (EHC) plan is. Which explanation is correct?
options: A school behaviour plan written by teachers
A health plan written by the GP
A legal local authority plan of needs and support
A voluntary plan that ends at 16
A.why: An EHC plan is a legal document issued by the local authority describing a child or young person's education, health and social care needs and provision, from birth to 25.

whyNot.0: Schools contribute, but the plan is issued by the local authority and is broader.
whyNot.1: Health advice contributes, but the local authority issues the plan.
whyNot.3: EHC plans are legal and can continue to 25.

A.q: Ava, 9, is autistic and does not use speech. She uses a picture symbol book. How should the nurse prepare her for a blood test?
options: Explain in simple speech to her mother
Use her symbol book to show each step
Do it quickly so she has less time to worry
Show her a video of another child
A.why: NG213: communicate using the child's preferred format, such as symbols or other AAC, giving time to process each step.

whyNot.0: Talking to her mother instead of Ava excludes her from her own care.
whyNot.3: A generic video does not use her own communication system.

B.q: Liam, 6, has cerebral palsy. The local authority has agreed to an EHC needs assessment. His parents ask how long the whole process should take. What should the nurse say?
options: No more than 6 weeks
No more than 20 weeks
No more than 12 months
No more than 16 weeks
B.why: SEND Code 9.40: from the request to issuing the final EHC plan must take no more than 20 weeks, subject to exemptions.

whyNot.0: Six weeks is the deadline for deciding whether to assess.
whyNot.2: Twelve months is the minimum review frequency for an existing plan.
whyNot.3: Sixteen weeks is the deadline for telling families if no plan will be issued.

B.q: A children's community nurse is asked to provide health advice for Maya's EHC needs assessment. By when must the advice be returned?
options: Within 2 weeks
Within 20 weeks
Within 6 weeks
Within 12 weeks
B.why: SEND Code 9.42: those asked for information for an EHC needs assessment must respond within a maximum of 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: Two weeks is shorter than the statutory maximum.
whyNot.1: Twenty weeks is the whole process, not the advice deadline.
whyNot.3: Twelve weeks is double the 6-week maximum set for advice in para 9.42.

B.q: Practitioners are writing the section of Maya's EHC plan that records her views. Maya, 14, uses symbols and drawings. What does NG213 say?
options: Summarise her views in professional language
Let her parents speak for her
Record her views in her own format and words
Record views once she can write them
B.why: NG213 1.4.13: preserve the child's voice: use their preferred format and their own words (or symbols, drawings), and do not rewrite them.

whyNot.0: Rewriting her words in professional language loses her voice.
whyNot.1: Parents contribute, but Maya's own views must be recorded.
whyNot.3: Non-written formats such as symbols and drawings are valid.

C.q: Noah, 12, is autistic with a learning disability and does not use speech. Over two days he has started banging his head and is more distressed than usual. What should the nurse do first?
options: Assess for a physical cause such as pain
Record it as part of his autism
Ask for a behaviour plan from psychology
Increase his sedative medicine
C.why: New distress or self-injury may be how a non-verbal child communicates pain or illness. Look for physical causes first to avoid diagnostic overshadowing.

whyNot.1: Attributing a change to autism risks missing pain or illness.
whyNot.2: Psychology input may help later, but a physical cause should be excluded first.
whyNot.3: Sedation could mask the cause and is not a first step.

C.q: Oscar, 8, is autistic and is distressed in the outpatient waiting area, covering his ears and rocking. His appointment is in 40 minutes. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Ask his parent to calm him in the waiting area
Move him to a quiet room until he is called
Rebook him for another day
Give him a tablet with loud cartoons
C.why: Reducing sensory overload, such as a quiet room away from the waiting area, is a reasonable adjustment that allows him to attend.

whyNot.0: The noisy environment remains the problem.
whyNot.2: Rebooking delays care when a simple adjustment would allow it today.
whyNot.3: Extra noise is likely to worsen sensory overload.

C.q: Jade, 2 years 6 months, used several words a year ago but now says none and has stopped responding to her name. What is the appropriate action?
options: Review at her next routine check
Refer to the autism team
Arrange a hearing test and wait
Advise more screen time with speech apps
C.why: NICE CG128 1.3.1: refer children under 3 with regression in language or social skills to the autism team (hearing should also be checked as part of assessment).

whyNot.0: Regression under 3 needs referral now, not at the next routine check.
whyNot.2: A hearing test is useful but should not delay referral for regression.
whyNot.3: Screen-based apps do not address regression and delay assessment.

reteach.title: Ask, adjust, advocate
reteach.question: How do you make care work for a child who experiences the world differently?

blocks.body: Ask: the child and family know the triggers, comforts and communication. Adjust: quiet spaces, visual timetables, the child's own communication format, less waiting. Advocate: contribute advice to the EHC plan within 6 weeks, record the child's own words, and look for a physical cause behind new distress.

blocks.text: Do not rewrite a child's words in the EHC plan to sound more 'professional'. NG213 says preserve their voice.

explain.body: Equality Act 2010 s20 places a duty on services to make reasonable adjustments so disabled people, including many autistic children, are not disadvantaged. Examples: quiet rooms, longer appointments, first or last appointment, visual supports.

test.q: Which law places a duty on NHS services to make reasonable adjustments for disabled children?
options: Children Act 1989
Mental Capacity Act 2005
Equality Act 2010
Human Rights Act 1998
test.why: The Equality Act 2010 s20 sets out the duty to make reasonable adjustments.

whyNot.0: The Children Act covers welfare and safeguarding, not reasonable adjustments.
whyNot.1: The MCA covers decision-making capacity from 16.
whyNot.3: The HRA protects rights but does not set out the reasonable adjustment duty.

explain.body: Ask whether the child has an up-to-date communication passport and record communication preferences in a shareable format, so the child does not have to repeat them (NG213 1.1.19–1.1.20).

test.q: A child with complex needs is admitted. What should the nurse ask about early to support communication?
options: Their most recent school reports
An up-to-date communication passport
Their current reading age
Their brothers' and sisters' views
test.why: NG213 1.1.19: ask if they have an up-to-date communication passport.

whyNot.0: School reports do not set out communication preferences.
whyNot.2: Reading age alone does not describe how the child communicates.
whyNot.3: Siblings may help, but the passport records the child's own preferences.

explain.body: LA decides on assessment within 6 weeks; professionals give advice within 6 weeks; if no plan, the family is told within 16 weeks; the final plan is issued within 20 weeks. Reviewed at least every 12 months.

test.q: How often must an EHC plan be reviewed by the local authority as a minimum?
options: Every 6 months
Every 3 years
Every 2 years
Every 12 months
test.why: SEND Code 9.166: EHC plans must be reviewed at least every 12 months.

whyNot.0: Six-monthly reviews are not the statutory minimum.
whyNot.1: Three years is far beyond the minimum.
whyNot.2: Two years is beyond the minimum.

explain.body: Diagnostic overshadowing is putting new symptoms down to a known condition, such as autism or learning disability, and missing a physical cause. A child who cannot describe pain may show it through behaviour change.

options: Attributing new symptoms to an existing diagnosis
Giving two diagnoses at the same time
Delaying diagnosis to avoid labelling
Making a diagnosis without the family
test.why: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing new signs or symptoms to an existing condition, so a physical problem is missed.

whyNot.2: Delaying to avoid labels is a different issue.
whyNot.3: Excluding the family is poor practice but not overshadowing.
